records.title: Power loom and mechanization of weaving
records.sourceNativeSummary: Cartwright's 1785 loom established powered weaving feasibility but his Doncaster mill failed financially; skilled mechanics improved the primitive design, patents were infringed, and by 1806 the principle had spread widely around Manchester. Technical principle, inventor business success and later diffusion therefore diverged.
records.rivalOrBoundary: Hand weaving remained superior enough for years that powered weaving lagged mechanized spinning.

sources.supports: patent, primitive design, failed mill, later diffusion
skilled mechanics/apprenticeship and distributed micro-invention context

records.title: Jacquard punched-card loom
records.sourceNativeSummary: Jacquard's 1804 mechanism built on prior automated-weaving work and externalized pattern instructions into interchangeable punched cards. It displaced the draw-boy bottleneck and made repeatable complex patterns much cheaper; the reusable representation later influenced computing designs.
records.rivalOrBoundary: It was an attachment/control innovation on weaving machinery, not a general computer, and it inherited earlier Vaucanson/Falcon mechanisms.

sources.supports: 1804 patent, prior work, punched-card mechanism and diffusion

records.title: Cort puddling and rolling
records.sourceNativeSummary: Cort's 1780s iron processes helped shift wrought-iron production toward coal-based puddling/rolling, but modern archival analysis shows the origin story is contested and should not be collapsed into a single heroic transfer claim. Process diffusion matters more than priority mythology.
records.rivalOrBoundary: Historical claims that Cort simply appropriated a complete Jamaican rolling innovation are disputed by surviving primary evidence; older forge routes continued.

sources.supports: archival evidence and disputed origin of Cort rolling

records.title: Neilson hot blast
records.sourceNativeSummary: Heating blast air sharply changed blast-furnace economics near the HD1 boundary, but recent metallurgy history challenges the clean 1828-Nielson-origin story and identifies earlier Botfield/Gilpin precedents. An effective industrial improvement can have distributed and retrospectively simplified origins.
records.rivalOrBoundary: Cold blast and earlier hot-air concepts were live alternatives; exact priority remains historically contested.

sources.supports: technical importance plus Botfield/Gilpin priority reappraisal
early historical account of hot-blast invention

records.title: Iron Bridge as structural cast-iron demonstration
records.sourceNativeSummary: The 1779 Iron Bridge answered a transport need while visibly demonstrating that large cast-iron structural members could be designed, fabricated and assembled. Its consequence depended on the surrounding Coalbrookdale ironmaking cluster and was partly demonstrative/advertising rather than a cheap universal bridge solution.
records.rivalOrBoundary: Stone/timber bridges remained practical alternatives; the bridge was expensive and structurally idiosyncratic.

sources.supports: construction, Darby/Pritchard context and industrial cluster

records.title: Coal-gas lighting as networked service
records.sourceNativeSummary: Murdoch's factory demonstrations proved coal gas could light buildings, but urban consequence required gas manufacture, pipes, burners, capital and a service organization. Winsor and chartered gas companies turned a local lighting technique into a networked utility.
records.rivalOrBoundary: Oil/candles and private on-site gas remained alternatives; gas hazards and network cost constrained adoption.

sources.supports: Murdoch, Winsor, public gas works and network diffusion

records.title: Fulton-Livingston operational steamboat service
records.sourceNativeSummary: Fulton was not the first steamboat experimenter. The 1807 Hudson voyage mattered because Fulton/Livingston combined prior experiments, capital and route organization into reliable commercial service; a successful demonstration was followed immediately by planning for scheduled operation.
records.rivalOrBoundary: Fitch, Rumsey, Stevens and others had working routes/prototypes earlier; commercial durability rather than priority defines this trajectory.

records.title: Erie Canal
records.sourceNativeSummary: The 1817-1825 Erie Canal used state finance and large-scale civil engineering to connect the Hudson with the Great Lakes. Its economic consequence came from a whole transport corridor and later feeder network, not a single lock/canal invention.
records.rivalOrBoundary: Routes and water-supply choices were political/geographic; canals later faced rail competition.

sources.supports: state funding, transport cost/time effect and canal-building diffusion

records.title: Macadam road construction
records.sourceNativeSummary: McAdam's road system around 1820 treated drainage, graded broken stone and maintainability as a repeatable road-building method rather than relying on massive foundations. The method improved all-weather transport but still demanded continuous maintenance.
records.rivalOrBoundary: Telford and older road-building methods used different structural principles; macadam was not maintenance-free.

sources.supports: layered stone/drainage method and maintenance requirement

records.title: Koenig steam-powered cylinder printing press
records.sourceNativeSummary: Koenig/Bauer converted printing from hand-press cycles into power-driven cylinder operation; The Times used the machines in 1814. The transition combined mechanism, steam power and a high-volume publication customer rather than an isolated prototype.
records.rivalOrBoundary: Hand presses remained useful for low-volume work; the surviving museum item is a later model, so primary performance claims need historical records rather than model appearance.

sources.supports: 1812 practical press and 1814 Times adoption history

records.title: Dalton atomic theory
records.sourceNativeSummary: Dalton's 1808 system used atomic weights and combination rules to organize chemistry quantitatively, but his assumed simplest formulas caused specific mistakes such as representing water as HO. A useful representational substrate improved chemical reasoning while containing wrong local claims.
records.rivalOrBoundary: Competing chemical representations remained; atom identity/formula inference was underdetermined by available evidence.

sources.supports: atomic theory, weights and historical limitations

records.title: Ørsted to Ampère electrodynamics
records.sourceNativeSummary: Ørsted's 1820 current-magnetism observation rapidly created a new experimental object; Ampère then formalized force relations and electrodynamic laws. Observation and mathematical representation advanced in quick succession rather than one replacing the other.
records.rivalOrBoundary: Initial qualitative effect did not by itself define a complete theory or practical electrical technology.

records.title: Laennec stethoscope
records.sourceNativeSummary: Laennec's 1816 instrument mediated internal chest sounds, making an otherwise inaccessible observation repeatable and correlatable with pathology. It spread rapidly across Europe/America, but interpretation required trained listening and post-mortem/clinical correlation.
records.rivalOrBoundary: Direct auscultation and subjective symptoms remained; an instrument improved observation but did not automatically make diagnosis true.

sources.supports: historical link between mediated auscultation and pathology

records.title: Isolation of quinine from cinchona
records.sourceNativeSummary: Long-standing Andean cinchona use preceded European chemistry. Pelletier and Caventou isolated quinine in 1820, converting a variable botanical remedy into a chemically defined active substance that could be standardized and studied separately from bark.
records.rivalOrBoundary: Isolation did not create the medicinal knowledge ex nihilo and did not solve later supply/extraction/colonial issues.

sources.supports: history of cinchona/quinine knowledge and standardization

records.title: Hutton's Siccar Point and deep time
records.sourceNativeSummary: Siccar Point's angular unconformity gave field evidence for deposition, deformation, erosion and renewed deposition over timescales far beyond simple recent-creation narratives. The crucial object was an observable sequence of processes, not merely Hutton's prose theory.
records.rivalOrBoundary: The observation constrained age/process narratives but did not fix modern numerical geologic time or every part of Hutton's Earth model.

records.title: Indian cotton textiles, British productivity advance and early deindustrialization pressure
records.sourceNativeSummary: India entered the eighteenth century as a major world textile exporter. By the early nineteenth century British manufacturing productivity, world-price changes, political fragmentation and colonial transfers jointly altered the competitive system; no single British machine explains the trajectory.
records.rivalOrBoundary: Causal attribution is explicitly multi-factor; later deindustrialization cannot be reduced to one tariff, one invention or one colonial mechanism.

sources.supports: 1765 onward relative-price evidence and domestic/foreign causal decomposition

records.title: Fairmount Water Works: steam route abandoned for water power
records.sourceNativeSummary: Philadelphia initially used steam pumping, but high operating costs, inefficiency and explosions drove the city to replace it with water wheels at Fairmount. A newer high-tech mechanism lost to an older power source under the local economic/safety world.
records.rivalOrBoundary: The failure was contextual, not proof that steam pumping was globally inferior.

sources.supports: steam cost/accident history and water-wheel replacement

records.title: Babbage Difference Engine integration failure
records.sourceNativeSummary: Babbage targeted error-prone mathematical tables with automatic finite-difference calculation. Government funding and Clement's precision engineering produced a working section, but the full 1820s design failed to close because cost, precision manufacture, contractor relations and design integration exceeded the institutional/project system; later construction from Babbage designs shows the core mechanism was not simply impossible.
records.rivalOrBoundary: Conceptual validity and project tractability diverged; later Difference Engine No.2 is not evidence that the original project could have closed cheaply in 1830.

sources.supports: table-error pressure, design, government cost, Clement dispute and later validation
scholarly history of Babbage/Airy institutional evaluation

records.title: Early steamboat false starts before durable service
records.sourceNativeSummary: Fitch, Rumsey, Symington and others produced materially different working steam-boat schemes before Fulton's durable service. Several demonstrations technically worked yet failed to obtain a repeatable economic/institutional route, showing that prototype motion and transport-system viability were distinct.
records.rivalOrBoundary: Priority disputes themselves can obscure differences between paddle, jet and towing systems.

sources.supports: Rumsey 1788 pamphlet, Fitch rivalry and distinct propulsion mechanisms
comparative history of Rumsey/Fitch experimental routes

records.title: Hot-air versus hydrogen balloons in 1783
records.sourceNativeSummary: Montgolfier hot-air balloons and Charles/Robert hydrogen balloons reached manned flight through different lift media in the same year. Both were technically valid; material availability, controllability, safety and use case—not a single scientific winner—shaped later balloon practice.
records.rivalOrBoundary: Balloon flight did not solve controlled heavier-than-air flight or reliable directional navigation.

sources.supports: parallel hydrogen route; used as secondary support only

records.title: Young/Fresnel wave optics
records.sourceNativeSummary: Young demonstrated interference and Fresnel independently extended diffraction/wave analysis before learning the full priority history. Their correspondence records correction, replication and credit rather than a single isolated discovery; diffraction evidence increasingly constrained corpuscular accounts.
records.rivalOrBoundary: Wave theory itself was revised later by electromagnetic/quantum physics; nineteenth-century success was domain-specific, not final ontology.

sources.supports: Fresnel 1816 letter acknowledging Young and describing diffraction experiments

records.title: Avogadro molecular hypothesis delayed acceptance
records.sourceNativeSummary: Avogadro's 1811 distinction between molecules and atoms offered a route through gas-volume/atomic-weight ambiguities, but it remained weakly adopted for decades because evidence, terminology and chemical assumptions did not yet force consensus. A productive representation can remain untractable without compatible measurement/conceptual infrastructure.
records.rivalOrBoundary: Later acceptance depended on Cannizzaro and improved atomic/molecular-weight reasoning outside HD1.

records.title: Cayley fixed-wing aerodynamic decomposition
records.sourceNativeSummary: By 1799 Cayley separated lift, propulsion and control in the fixed-wing aircraft concept and by 1804 flew a model glider, but engines/material/control capabilities adequate for powered flight were missing. The representation was useful decades before the full intervention path became tractable.
records.rivalOrBoundary: Correct conceptual decomposition did not provide sufficient power-to-weight, structural or control technology.

records.title: U.S. federal patent system
records.sourceNativeSummary: The 1790 U.S. patent statute created a federal examination mechanism and granted the first patent that July; the institution tried to convert invention disclosure into time-bounded property rights. Whitney's later cotton-gin experience shows legal specification did not guarantee practical appropriation or prevent copying.
records.rivalOrBoundary: Patent existence is not evidence that a technology is useful, novel in every historical sense, or economically capturable.

sources.supports: 1790 statute, first Patent Board and first U.S. patent

records.title: École Polytechnique and organized engineering education
records.sourceNativeSummary: Created in 1794 amid state need for technically trained engineers/officials, École Polytechnique institutionalized a broad mathematics/physics/chemistry foundation feeding specialized public-works schools. It changed the production and transmission of engineering capability rather than solving one technical task.
records.rivalOrBoundary: Formal schools complemented rather than instantly replaced apprenticeship, workshops and military/civil corps traditions.

sources.supports: contrast/complement with apprenticeship-based British skill production

records.title: Factory child labor and unenforced early Acts
records.sourceNativeSummary: The 1802 and 1819 Acts recognized extreme child/apprentice labor conditions and specified age/hour/education constraints, but inspection/enforcement remained weak. A written rule therefore existed without reliable physical consequence until later inspector institutions.
records.rivalOrBoundary: This is a governance/effect case, not a claim that regulation itself was technically sufficient.

sources.supports: legislative chronology and later inspector contrast

records.title: Davy/Stephenson miners' safety lamps
records.sourceNativeSummary: Firedamp explosions created an urgent mine-safety pressure. Davy's wire-gauze lamp and Stephenson's independently developed lamp embodied different routes; the devices reduced flame propagation risk, but low light, user incentives, ventilation and false confidence meant a safety mechanism could create new operating behavior rather than eliminate danger.
records.rivalOrBoundary: Priority was disputed and later lamps combined design ideas; safety depended on mine system/ventilation, not lamp possession alone.

sources.supports: surviving early Davy lamps and mechanism/history
safety-lamp use, limits and operational context

records.title: Skilled mechanics, apprenticeship and micro-invention networks
records.sourceNativeSummary: Archival reconstruction of hundreds of British mechanics shows industrial improvement was carried by apprenticeship, workshop mobility and many small modifications that often never became famous patents. This invisible capability substrate linked named inventions and made implementation/recombination possible.
records.rivalOrBoundary: It does not imply patents or formal science were irrelevant; it corrects an inventor-only sample frame.
